title: ATM
scopeHtml: Scope: requirements, session state, chain-of-responsibility cash dispenser with plan-then-commit, runnable Java and Kotlin, account-level atomicity and idempotency, follow-ups. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Design an ATM: insert card, enter PIN, check balance, withdraw cash.

Functional:

  • Card inserted, then PIN (3 wrong attempts ejects the card), then a session.
  • Balance enquiry and cash withdrawal in notes of 2000, 500 and 100.
  • Withdraw succeeds only if the account has enough money and the machine can make the exact amount from the notes it holds.
  • Notes leave the machine only after the account is debited.

Non-functional: the order of operations must never give free cash or take money without paying; the account is shared (many ATMs, apps).

Worked example. Account has 5,000. Withdraw 3,700 with notes 2000, 500, 100 available: plan = one 2000, three 500 (1500), two 100 (200) = 3,700. Debit leaves 1,300. A request for 150 fails because no combination of 100s makes it, and the account is NOT debited.

Industry examples. Real ATMs (NCR, Diebold Nixdorf) talk the ISO 8583 message protocol to the bank's switch; banks authorise and debit on their side, and the ATM dispenses only after approval. Indian UPI/IMPS back ends use idempotency keys so a retry after a network timeout never double-debits.

Everyday analogy. A shopkeeper who first checks the cash drawer can make the exact change, then takes your money, and only then hands over the goods.

Common interview traps.

  • Dispensing cash before the debit is confirmed (or debiting before checking the machine can pay).
  • Forgetting the PIN retry limit and card ejection.

notes.title: Core entities
notes.html:
• Account: id, PIN (a hash in real life), balance in minor units, debit and credit.
  • Bank: finds accounts; in reality a remote service (the ATM is a thin client).
  • NoteHandler chain and Dispenser: how cash is made.
  • ATM: session state (IDLE, CARD_IN, AUTHENTICATED) and the operations.

Plan, then commit. The dispenser first computes a plan (which notes) without changing anything, the account is debited, then the plan is committed to the cash counts. That order means a failed plan never costs the customer money, and a failed debit never loses cash. If the machine crashes between debit and dispense, a real ATM writes a journal and the bank reverses the transaction on reconciliation.

Decision gravity. The ATM is a thin client of the bank (the bank owns the balance): a one-way door you must keep, since money lives in one place. The dispenser's greedy algorithm (largest note first) is correct for canonical sets like 2000/500/100 but not for arbitrary denominations; changing to dynamic programming later is a local, reversible change.

Everyday analogy. A vending machine with a bank behind it: counts what it holds, asks the bank for permission, then dispenses.

Common interview traps.

  • Storing the PIN in plain text or logging it.
  • Money as double; use long in paise or cents.

notes.title: Class diagram
notes.html:
+--------------------------+       +----------------+
 | ATM                      |------>| Bank           |
 |  state: AtmState         | uses  |  find(id)      |
 |  current: Account        |       +-------+--------+
 |  insertCard, enterPin,   |               | has many
 |  balance, withdraw, eject|               v
 +------------+-------------+       +----------------+
              | uses                | Account        |
              v                     |  id, pin       |
 +--------------------------+       |  balance       |
 | Dispenser                |       |  debit/credit  |
 |  plan(amt), commit(plan) |       +--------^-------+
 +------------+-------------+                |
              | head                  SafeAccount (synchronized)
              v
 +--------------+  next  +--------------+  next  +--------------+
 | Notes 2000   |------->| Notes 500    |------->| Notes 100    |
 +--------------+        +--------------+        +--------------+
                 (Chain of Responsibility)

 enum AtmState { IDLE, CARD_IN, AUTHENTICATED }
 IDLE --insertCard--> CARD_IN --enterPin ok--> AUTHENTICATED --eject--> IDLE

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing the cash-handling logic into the ATM class.
  • No state guard: calling withdraw before authentication.

notes.title: Key patterns
notes.html:
• State (session). Operations are legal only in certain states. An enum plus a require(state) guard is enough here; a full State class per state is the same shape as the vending machine and can be used if the flow grows (PIN change, deposit).
  • Chain of Responsibility (notes). Each handler takes what it can and passes the rest. Why: adding a 200 note is one new handler. Alternative: a loop over a sorted list of denominations (shorter, equally good; say so).
  • Facade. ATM hides Bank, Dispenser and state.
  • Proxy/Adapter (optional). Bank is an interface to the remote core banking system.
  • Command/Memento for the journal (optional). Each transaction as an object so it can be logged and reversed.

Industry examples. Java servlet filters and Express/OkHttp interceptors are chains of responsibility. Payment systems (Stripe, Razorpay) use idempotency keys plus a transaction journal for exactly the crash window described above.

Everyday analogy. Paying with change: hand over the biggest bills first, then smaller ones for the rest.

Common interview traps.

  • Over-using patterns when a sorted list and a loop is clearer.
  • Greedy that fails on non-canonical denominations; state the assumption.

notes.title: Code
notes.html:
Java (compiled and run with JDK 21):

import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.*;

class Account {
    final String id; final String pin;
    protected long balance;
    Account(String id, String pin, long balance) { this.id = id; this.pin = pin; this.balance = balance; }
    long balance() { return balance; }
    /** Check-then-act: NOT safe when two ATMs hit the same account (see Concurrency). */
    boolean debit(long amt) {
        if (amt <= 0 || balance < amt) return false;
        balance -= amt; return true;
    }
    void credit(long amt) { balance += amt; }
}

class Bank {
    protected final Map<String, Account> accounts = new HashMap<>();
    void add(Account a) { accounts.put(a.id, a); }
    Account find(String id) { return accounts.get(id); }
}

/** Chain of Responsibility: each handler dispenses as many notes of its value as it can, then passes the rest on. */
abstract class NoteHandler {
    final int value; int count; NoteHandler next;
    NoteHandler(int value, int count) { this.value = value; this.count = count; }
    /** Plan only (no mutation): fills `out` and returns true if exact amount can be made. */
    boolean plan(long amt, Map<Integer, Integer> out) {
        int use = (int) Math.min(count, amt / value);
        long rest = amt - (long) use * value;
        if (use > 0) out.put(value, use);
        if (rest == 0) return true;
        return next != null && next.plan(rest, out);
    }
    void commit(Map<Integer, Integer> plan) {
        count -= plan.getOrDefault(value, 0);
        if (next != null) next.commit(plan);
    }
}
class Notes extends NoteHandler { Notes(int v, int c) { super(v, c); } }

class Dispenser {
    private final NoteHandler head;
    Dispenser(NoteHandler... hs) {                    // pass the biggest note first
        for (int i = 0; i + 1 < hs.length; i++) hs[i].next = hs[i + 1];
        head = hs[0];
    }
    Optional<Map<Integer, Integer>> plan(long amt) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> out = new TreeMap<>(Comparator.reverseOrder());
        return head.plan(amt, out) ? Optional.of(out) : Optional.empty();
    }
    void commit(Map<Integer, Integer> p) { head.commit(p); }
}

enum AtmState { IDLE, CARD_IN, AUTHENTICATED }

class ATM {
    private final Bank bank; private final Dispenser cash;
    private AtmState state = AtmState.IDLE;
    private Account current; private int badPins = 0;

    ATM(Bank bank, Dispenser cash) { this.bank = bank; this.cash = cash; }

    void insertCard(String accountId) {
        require(AtmState.IDLE);
        current = bank.find(accountId);
        if (current == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown card");
        state = AtmState.CARD_IN; badPins = 0;
    }
    boolean enterPin(String pin) {
        require(AtmState.CARD_IN);
        if (current.pin.equals(pin)) { state = AtmState.AUTHENTICATED; return true; }
        if (++badPins >= 3) eject();                  // swallow/eject after 3 tries
        return false;
    }
    long balance() { require(AtmState.AUTHENTICATED); return current.balance(); }

    Map<Integer, Integer> withdraw(long amt) {
        require(AtmState.AUTHENTICATED);
        Map<Integer, Integer> plan = cash.plan(amt)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalStateException("ATM cannot make " + amt));
        if (!current.debit(amt)) throw new IllegalStateException("insufficient funds");
        cash.commit(plan);                            // notes leave only after the debit succeeded
        return plan;
    }
    void eject() { state = AtmState.IDLE; current = null; }
    AtmState state() { return state; }
    private void require(AtmState s) { if (state != s) throw new IllegalStateException("state is " + state + ", need " + s); }
}

Kotlin core (hand translated, not compiled in this session):

class Account(val id: String, private val pin: String, private var balance: Long) {
    @Synchronized fun balance() = balance
    @Synchronized fun debit(amt: Long): Boolean {
        if (amt <= 0 || balance < amt) return false
        balance -= amt; return true
    }
    fun pinOk(p: String) = pin == p
}

/** Greedy plan, largest note first; returns null if the exact amount cannot be made. */
class Dispenser(private val notes: MutableMap<Int, Int>) {       // note value -> count, e.g. 2000 to 10
    fun plan(amt: Long): Map<Int, Int>? {
        var rest = amt
        val out = linkedMapOf<Int, Int>()
        for ((value, count) in notes.toSortedMap(reverseOrder())) {
            val use = minOf(count.toLong(), rest / value).toInt()
            if (use > 0) { out[value] = use; rest -= use.toLong() * value }
        }
        return if (rest == 0L) out else null
    }
    fun commit(plan: Map<Int, Int>) = plan.forEach { (v, n) -> notes[v] = notes.getValue(v) - n }
}

enum class AtmState { IDLE, CARD_IN, AUTHENTICATED }

class Atm(private val accounts: Map<String, Account>, private val cash: Dispenser) {
    var state = AtmState.IDLE; private set
    private var current: Account? = null

    fun withdraw(amt: Long): Map<Int, Int> {
        check(state == AtmState.AUTHENTICATED) { "not authenticated" }
        val plan = cash.plan(amt) ?: error("ATM cannot make $amt")
        check(current!!.debit(amt)) { "insufficient funds" }
        cash.commit(plan)                                  // notes leave only after the debit
        return plan
    }
}

Choices: plan does not mutate, so it can be retried; the greedy chain returns "cannot make" for 150 because only 100s are left. The PIN is compared as a plain string for brevity only; production stores a salted hash and the bank verifies it (the ATM never knows it).

Common interview traps.

  • Mutating note counts during planning, then failing halfway and leaving the machine inconsistent.
  • Allowing debit(0) or negative amounts.

notes.title: Run and test
notes.html:
public class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Bank bank = new Bank();
        bank.add(new SafeAccount("acc1", "1234", 5_000));
        Dispenser cash = new Dispenser(new Notes(2000, 10), new Notes(500, 10), new Notes(100, 10));
        ATM atm = new ATM(bank, cash);
        atm.insertCard("acc1");
        System.out.println("wrong pin ok? " + atm.enterPin("0000"));      // false
        System.out.println("right pin ok? " + atm.enterPin("1234"));      // true
        System.out.println("notes for 3700 = " + atm.withdraw(3700));     // {2000=1, 500=3, 100=2}
        System.out.println("balance = " + atm.balance());                  // 1300
        try { atm.withdraw(150); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("error: " + e.getMessage()); }
        atm.eject();

        // 10 ATMs, same account with 1000, each withdraws 200: exactly 5 may succeed
        Account shared = new SafeAccount("acc2", "1", 1_000);
        ExecutorService ex = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10);
        CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1);
        List<Future<Boolean>> fs = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) fs.add(ex.submit(() -> { go.await(); return shared.debit(200); }));
        go.countDown();
        int ok = 0; for (Future<Boolean> f : fs) if (f.get()) ok++;
        ex.shutdown();
        System.out.println("successful = " + ok + ", balance = " + shared.balance());   // 5, 0
    }
}

Actual output from javac Demo.java && java Demo:

wrong pin ok? false
right pin ok? true
notes for 3700 = {2000=1, 500=3, 100=2}
balance = 1300
error: ATM cannot make 150
successful = 5, balance = 0

The last line is the concurrency test: ten threads each withdraw 200 from 1,000; exactly five succeed and the balance ends at 0, never negative.

Common interview traps.

  • Not testing: wrong PIN thrice, not enough cash in machine, not enough balance, withdraw before login.
  • Asserting only the happy path.

notes.title: Concurrency
notes.html:
The shared resource is the account, not the ATM. The same account can be debited from several ATMs, a mobile app and an auto-debit at the same time. debit is check-then-act: it reads balance >= amt, then subtracts. Two threads with balance 1,000 and amt 800 can both pass the check and drive the balance to -600.

Fix options, with gravity:

  1. synchronized on the account (below): correct inside one JVM, trivial to reason about.
  2. AtomicLong with a compare-and-set loop: lock-free on a single value.
  3. Database: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - ? WHERE id = ? AND balance >= ? and check that one row changed; or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE in a transaction. This is the real answer, because the account lives in a database shared by many servers, where JVM locks do nothing.
class SafeAccount extends Account {
    SafeAccount(String id, String pin, long bal) { super(id, pin, bal); }
    @Override synchronized boolean debit(long amt) { return super.debit(amt); }   // check + subtract together
    @Override synchronized void credit(long amt) { super.credit(amt); }
    @Override synchronized long balance() { return super.balance(); }
}
// Cash in a real ATM is one physical machine with one user, so Dispenser needs no lock.
// The shared thing is the ACCOUNT (many ATMs, mobile app, UPI): that is where the lock (or a DB row lock) lives.

Idempotency. If the ATM times out after sending a debit, it does not know whether it happened. Give each withdrawal a unique transaction id; the bank stores processed ids and returns the original result on a retry, so a retry never debits twice.

Symptom in production. Negative balances or a customer debited with no cash dispensed. Metrics: accounts with balance < 0, count of debits with no matching dispense in the journal.

Everyday analogy. Two cashiers drawing from the same till: each must look at the till and take cash in one uninterrupted motion.

Common interview traps.

  • Locking the ATM but not the account.
  • Synchronising in Java and thinking it works across servers.
  • Locking two accounts in different orders for a transfer (deadlock); order locks by account id.

notes.title: Follow-ups
notes.html:
• Deposit and transfer. Transfers lock two accounts in id order, or do both updates in one DB transaction.
  • Daily withdrawal limit. Another check in withdraw; store the day's total on the account.
  • Denominations that are not canonical. Replace greedy with a bounded coin-change DP.
  • Out-of-cash and fraud. An OUT_OF_SERVICE state; velocity checks at the bank.
  • Receipts and audit log. A journal written before dispensing, replayed on restart.
  • Security. PIN as a hash verified by the bank; encrypted PIN block; lock after 3 attempts.

Common interview traps.

  • Answering "how to scale" with locks; across servers the answer is the database's atomicity plus idempotency.
  • Ignoring the crash window between debit and dispense.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Flow: insert card, PIN (3 tries), authenticated session, operations, eject. Session guarded by an enum state.
  • Cash dispensing is a chain of handlers with a plan-then-commit order; debit happens between plan and commit.
  • Money is an integer in minor units; PIN is never stored in plain text in real systems.
  • Concurrency: the shared object is the account; make check-and-subtract atomic (lock in a JVM, conditional UPDATE in a database) and make retries idempotent.
  • Extensions: transfers (lock ordering), limits, non-canonical notes (DP), audit journal.
